---

When it is cold, it stinks—and not till then.
The seasonable, more feverish heats
Of love and summer in some other cities
Unseal the all-too-human; not in his.
When it is cold, it stinks, but not before;
It smells to high heaven, most creaturely,
When it is cold. It stinks, but not before
His freezing eye has worked its utmost harm—
To sever limbs, livelihood, and name,
Abstracting life beyond all likelihood.
When it is cold, it stinks, and not till then
Can it turn fragrant. On canal and street,
Colder and colder, Murphy gives way to Molloy,
The weather hardens round the Idiot Boy,
That gleeful hero of the long retreat.
When he is cold, he stinks, but not before—
This living corpse. The existential weather
Is scented in these abortive minims, men
Who, barely living, therefore live entire
Until they die; and sweetly smell till then.

---

I preserved the recursive, incantatory structure (the repeated "when it is cold it stinks" refrain), all literary allusions (Murphy, Molloy, the Idiot Boy), and the poem's central conceit linking coldness, decay, and existential diminishment. Only in frigid conditions does the odor emerge—never otherwise. In other places, the fervent or feverish passions of love and summer might reveal what is genuinely human, but not here. The stench arrives solely with the chill, most intensely revealing raw mortality precisely when temperatures drop. Yet the smell waits until his icy stare has thoroughly wreaked its damage—severing limbs, destroying livelihoods, erasing identity, stripping existence down to something scarcely recognizable as life at all.

Fragrance becomes possible only through cold's arrival. Along waterways and thoroughfares, as temperatures continue their descent, the journey moves from Murphy toward Molloy, and the atmosphere solidifies around the Idiot Boy—that joyful protagonist of the extended withdrawal.

This animated corpse emits its odor only in coldness, never sooner. The philosophical climate reveals itself through these incomplete, diminished beings—men whose existence remains so tenuous that they achieve genuine life only in dying; and until that moment arrives, they retain their sweetness.
outputs.L3:
# On Cold as Revelation: An Analysis of the Poem's Central Paradox

The poem's haunting refrain—"when it is cold it stinks, but not before"—functions as more than a mere observation about decay; it establishes an entire cosmology in which cold, rather than warmth, becomes the threshold condition through which hidden truths about existence are revealed. This inversion demands our attention, for it upends a deeply embedded literary convention.

## Subverting the Traditional Symbolism of Heat

In the traditional literary imagination, particularly in narratives of urban life, summer heat and its attendant passions serve as the great revealer of human nature. Cities swelter, tempers flare, love affairs bloom and curdle, and in that fevered atmosphere, characters shed their pretenses to reveal what lies beneath. The heat acts as a kind of confessional pressure, forcing truth to the surface through sheer thermal intensity.

This poem, however, constructs an entirely different world—one where such conventions are inverted. Here, it is coldness, not heat, that "unseals the all too human." The very phrase suggests something sealed shut, preserved, held in stasis—until cold arrives to crack that seal and expose what lies within. Where heat might be expected to cause things to fester and reveal themselves through decomposition and stench, this poem insists on the opposite: warmth conceals, cold exposes.

## The Violence of the Freezing Eye

Central to this cold cosmology is the image of a harsh "freezing eye"—a gaze that does not merely observe but actively diminishes. This is no passive winter; it is an agent of amputation, severing limbs, livelihood, and identity itself. The freezing eye works with a terrible efficiency, stripping away the accoutrements of living *before* the stench of mortality can even fully emerge. This is crucial to understanding the poem's logic: death's characteristic odor, that final proof of decay, requires warmth to develop. The freezing eye, therefore, performs a kind of pre-emptive violence—diminishing the human before the body has even had the chance to complete its final biological betrayal.

## Beckett's Shadow: The Long Retreat

The poem's allusions to Beckett-like figures—evoking Murphy, Molloy, the Idiot Boy—summon an entire tradition of existential decline. These are not heroic figures marching toward glorious ends but shuffling, diminished beings engaged in what the poem terms a "long retreat." This retreat unfolds across a landscape that is itself hardening, freezing, becoming inhospitable to the very continuation of life. The Beckettian resonance is apt: these figures exist in a state of attenuated being, reduced to their barest essentials, moving not toward triumph but toward a kind of bleak diminishment that mirrors the poem's central thermal metaphor.

## The Paradox of Abortive Minims

The poem's closing movement crystallizes its central paradox through the figure of "abortive minims"—barely-living entities who are, in musical notation, brief notes cut short before their full duration. These abortive minims achieve full inhabitation of life only through the act of dying itself; existence and its ending become paradoxically intertwined. Most strikingly, they remain "sweetly" fragrant only until the cold sets in—suggesting that their brief moment of sweetness, of recognizable humanity, exists in that liminal space before the freezing eye does its work.

This final paradox brings the poem's logic full circle: warmth preserves a kind of sweetness, a fullness of being, while cold—far from simply killing—reveals the truth that was always latent within that sweetness. The stench that "was not before" cold arrived was never truly absent; it was merely unsealed, waiting for the freezing eye to strip away the illusions of warmth and expose what mortality had concealed all along.

# The Frozen Bloom: On Decay, Cold, and the Fragrance of Dying

There is a peculiar architecture to suffering when it is rendered poetically—a structure that loops back upon itself, that repeats not for emphasis but because repetition is the only honest response to an existence that offers no forward motion, only the same cold recursions of decline. This is the territory the text inhabits: a landscape built from refrains, where language circles around the body's betrayal rather than narrating any escape from it.

Murphy shuffles through these pages less as a character than as a condition—a body that has already surrendered its warmth before the narrative even begins. He is not dying; he has arrived, somehow, already on the other side of vitality, existing in a present tense that feels borrowed from the past. Molloy, likewise, drags himself forward not through will but through sheer biological inertia, his decay so total that motion itself seems like an afterthought, a habit the body performs out of some residual, meaningless loyalty to continuation. And then there is the Idiot Boy—perhaps the most devastating of these figures—whose very designation strips him of interiority before he can claim any, who exists as pure symptom, pure diminishment, a body without the scaffolding of comprehension to make sense of its own falling apart.

These are not characters in decline; they are declensions given flesh. The text insists, through its circling repetitions, that deterioration is not something that happens *to* these figures over time—it is their fundamental condition, the ground state from which they never departed. There was no vitality to lose. There was only ever the slow performance of a life that had already, in some essential sense, ended before it started.

And yet—here is the text's cruel, luminous insight—it is precisely in this deterioration, in the coldness that settles into limbs and language alike, that something like truth finally emerges. These are, the text suggests, *living corpses*: bodies that walk and speak and shuffle while already carrying the chemical signature of their own ending. And corpses, as anyone who has encountered death knows, do not smell of nothing. They smell, eventually, unmistakably—of something almost sweet, almost fragrant, a scent that arrives only after the struggle of pretending to be alive has ceased.

This is the paradox the text stages again and again, in its hypnotic, incantatory repetitions: that authenticity is not available to the living in their vital, striving state. It arrives instead as residue, as by-product, as the exhaust of a body finally admitting what it always was. The fragrance is not a symbol of life triumphant but of life finally *stopped*—the cessation that allows, at last, some genuine essence to escape the body's failed performance of continuing.

To be truly present, in this vision, is to have suffered enough, declined enough, grown cold enough that the mask of vitality can no longer be sustained. Murphy's stillness, Molloy's crawling, the Idiot Boy's blank incomprehension—these are not failures to live but the necessary unravelings that precede any authentic emanation. The sweetness comes only when the struggle ends. The fragrance blooms only in the frost. And existence, in this bleak arithmetic, is most itself only in the moment it ceases to insist upon itself at all.
outputs.L5:
# When The Seal Breaks

When ancient things stir, the world takes notice. There exists a particular moment—brief, charged, irreversible—when the boundary between what was hidden and what is revealed simply ceases to exist. This is the moment of unsealing.

Throughout history, humanity has been drawn to the seal: the wax stamp on a royal decree, the stone door of a forgotten tomb, the vault holding secrets too dangerous for common eyes. The seal represents restraint, a promise that certain things should remain undisturbed until the proper time. But seals are not permanent. They are, by their very nature, temporary guardians—waiting for the hand, the key, or the circumstance that will finally break them.

When we speak of unsealing, we speak of transformation. The unsealing of an old letter reveals words meant for someone long gone. The unsealing of a legal document releases information that reshapes lives. The unsealing of a container—whether a jar of preserves or a chamber of forgotten history—exposes what time and intention have kept separate from the present.

There is often fear surrounding the unsealed. What was contained, after all, may have been contained for reason. Yet there is equally a deep human curiosity, a pull toward discovery that outweighs caution. When the seal finally gives way, something changes—not just in the object itself, but in the one who breaks it. Knowledge, once released, cannot be resealed. The unsealing marks a threshold crossed, a truth no longer withheld.

Perhaps this is why the moment of unsealing captures our imagination so completely: it is the instant when waiting ends, when the hidden becomes known, when the story—whatever it may be—finally begins to unfold.

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a poem in the style of a villanelle-like refrain structure about decay, cold, and mortality, referencing Beckett's characters Murphy and Molloy.
counterfactuals.output:
# What the Cold Remembers

*(a villanelle for Murphy and Molloy)*

In Murphy's mind the world at last grows cold,
a system closing like a fist on dust—
Molloy forgets the roads his mother told.

The rocking chair stands empty, growing old,
the flesh subtracts itself until it must
—in Murphy's mind the world at last grows cold.

Stones keep the silence flesh has always told,
before it learned that trust becomes a crust—
Molloy forgets the roads his mother told.

No mercy waits for those who lie controlled
by hungers that no kindness can adjust—
in Murphy's mind the world at last grows cold.

The ditch, the crutch, the body growing old,
still crawling toward a silence it can trust—
Molloy forgets the roads his mother told.

So let the cold undo what once was bold:
in Murphy's mind the world at last grows cold,
Molloy forgets the roads his mother told,
and dust to dust returns, as dust it must.
counterfactuals.label: cf_1

counterfactuals.prompt: Compose a literary poem exploring the theme "when it is cold it stinks" as a metaphor for existential decline, using repetition and allusions to Samuel Beckett's novels.
counterfactuals.output:
**When It Is Cold It Stinks**

When it is cold it stinks—
the way a ditch stinks
when a man like Molloy
lies down in it, sucking his stones,
counting them wrong,
counting them right,
counting them anyway
because counting is warmer than dying,
though dying is what the cold is for.

When it is cold it stinks,
the way a room stinks
where Malone waits
with his exercise book,
his pencil worn to a stub of grammar,
writing himself into someone else
because a man alone in a bed
is still a man, still stinking,
still cold, still writing
the story of the story
of the man who is cold.

When it is cold it stinks—
say it again, it stinks—
the unnamable said it best,
the voice without a mouth,
the mouth without a face,
saying *I can't go on*
in a jar that has no seasons,
only degrees of gray,
only the temperature of never,
saying *I'll go on*
because stinking is a kind of motion,
and motion is a kind of hope,
thin as a coat in November.

When it is cold it stinks
like a bicycle rusting in a hedge,
like a body that forgets its bicycle,
like a name that forgets its body,
Molloy, Malone, the one who has no name—
all of them cold,
all of them stinking,
all of them going on
because there is no version of ending
that isn't also a kind of weather.

When it is cold it stinks.
Say it until it means nothing.
Say it until it means everything—
the way the trilogy means nothing,
means everything,
a man in a ditch,
a man in a bed,
a voice in a jar,
each one a degree colder
than the one before,
each one stinking
of the same unfinished sentence:

*I can't go on. I'll go on.*
It is cold.
It stinks.
Go on.
counterfactuals.label: cf_2

counterfactuals.prompt: Create a dense, philosophical poem with recurring lines about cold and stink, weaving in references to "the Idiot Boy" and Beckett's fiction to evoke a bleak, absurdist tone.
counterfactuals.output:
**The Cold That Names Us**

The cold does not forgive; the stink insists—
this is the first fact, before the moon
mistook a pond for lanterns, before Betty Foy
sent her fool son riding through the dark
to fetch a doctor who will not arrive.
He rides. He always rides. Johnny on the pony,
laughing at owls, at nothing, at the shape
his shadow makes against the hedge—
he is the joy that reason cannot use,
he is the cold; he is himself the stink
of a world that spoils before it's given.

*

Molloy sucks stones and swaps them pocket to pocket,
a rule invented only to be kept,
the way we keep the cold, the way we keep
the smell of our own rotting reasoned out.
Malone dies and does not stop reporting.
The Unnamable insists it has no mouth
yet goes on speaking through the stink of ink—
a voice that will not end because an ending
implies a purpose, and there is no purpose,
only the cold that will not forgive,
only the stink that will not clarify.

*

What is philosophy but a longer ride
into a night that will not answer back?
Watt counts his spoons and cannot make them add;
the idiot boy can't tell the hour by the clock
but knows the pony's warmth, the owl's cold cry—
knows, perhaps, more than our knowing does,
being no wiser than the frost, and thus
its equal, undeceived, and unafraid.
The cold does not forgive. The stink persists
in every mattress, every ditch, every
comedy of bodies failing on cue.

*

Say the boy is God's fool, or say he's nothing;
say the crawling man is Christ, or say he's meat—
it makes no difference to the frost that holds
the field, the breath, the moment before it fails.
Betty Foy waits by a window turned to glass
by cold that does not care whom it composes.
Molloy crawls his ditch call it devotion,
call it the only sentence left to finish.

*

We ride, we crawl, we count our stones, our spoons,
we stink of trying, and the trying's cold,
and nothing waits at the end but more of this:
the cold that will not forgive, the stink that stays,
the idiot joy of moving anyway—
not toward an answer, not away from dark,
but the way a wheel goes on because it's round,
the way a voice goes on because it's there,
the way the cold, the stink, the idiot, and the tale
all fail together, brightly, without end.
counterfactuals.label: cf_3

counterfactuals.prompt: Draft a formal poem employing anaphora and Beckettian imagery (Murphy, Molloy) to meditate on the corporeal decay of the human condition in wintry, existential terms.
counterfactuals.output:
# The Body's Winter Catechism

*after Murphy, after Molloy*

I who have crawled through ditches to become the ditch,
I who have counted my teeth with a tongue grown foreign,
I who have named each ache a small dominion—
I persist, though the persisting is a kind of falling.

I who have watched the fingers curl like paper in slow fire,
I who have felt the knee forget its ancient covenant with walking,
I who have heard the joints converse in their dry Latin—
I persist, though persistence wears the face of ending.

I who have lain as Murphy lay, rocking in his chair of ropes,
I who have sought the zero of the mind's dark room,
I who have found the body will not be so easily excused—
I persist, a garrison manning a fort already fallen.

I who have gone as Molloy went, on bicycle, on crutch, on belly,
I who have measured miles by the failing of the legs,
I who have made of my decline a kind of pilgrimage—
I persist toward no shrine but the one that waits in all of us.

I who have felt December enter through the marrow,
I who have watched my breath hang visible as a doubt,
I who have understood the cold as an argument, unanswerable—
I persist, though the season keeps its terrible appointment.

I who am less each morning than the night before,
I who am a subtraction working toward its sum,
I who am the winter's patient, unfinished sentence—
I persist. I persist. The word is all the warmth there is.

Snow does not fall so much as it arrives,
already having fallen, always having been falling,
the way the body was always this rehearsal
for the stillness it was born already halfway toward.

I who write this with a hand that trembles like a leaf
still arguing its case against the branch—
I persist, in the old absurd rebellion,
the "I can't go on" that goes on, that goes on, that goes on.
counterfactuals.label: cf_4

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a highly literary, allusive poem that repeats the phrase "when it is cold it stinks" as a structural device, exploring themes of mortality, freezing, and living death, with nods to Beckett and Wordsworth's "Idiot Boy."
counterfactuals.output:
# The Cold Testament

When it is cold it stinks—the frost is honest,
unlike the summer's perfumed alibi
that hides the meat's slow conference with worms.
Johnny rides his pony through the night, his mother
calling *Johnny, Johnny* to the moon
that doesn't answer, being long past caring,
being a stone that learned indifference early.

When it is cold it stinks the way a mouth stinks
that has stopped forming words worth freezing for.
Godot, they tell me, isn't coming. Fine.
I'll wait here with the idiot boy and the owls,
count vowels like Vladimir counts his hours,
each one a small rehearsal for the last.

*I grow old, I grow old,* someone else said,
in warmer rooms, with peaches, with the luxury
of ripening. But here the pond has skinned
itself in silver, and the fish beneath
go on their business in a kind of tomb
that isn't quite a tomb—call it a waiting.

When it is cold it stinks like Nagg and Nell
in their identical bins, remembering
Lake Como, sunlight, anything but this—
this now, this here, this endless little now
that Wordsworth's boy would recognize as time
before we learned to lie about its shape.

The betty at the door says *tell me true,*
but truth in winter has a rancid edge,
the way a held breath, finally let go,
comes out as fog—as if the soul itself
were visible at last, and visibly
a kind of steam that can't decide to leave.

When it is cold it stinks. I say it now
the third time, structural, the way a bell
insists on its own bronze, its one dumb note
that means *remember* and means nothing else.
The pony clops. The tramps remain unmoved.
The idiot laughs at nothing, which is wise—

for nothing is the thing that waits for us
in every room we haven't entered yet,
patient as snow, indifferent as the moon,
and when it comes—it always comes—it stinks
the way all honest reckonings must stink:
not evil, just undressed. Just cold. Just here.
counterfactuals.label: cf_5
